To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) fixational saccadic direction is biased toward parafoveal but not peripheral stimuli; 2) the rate of fixational eye movements toward parafoveal targets increases with parafoveal target contrast; and 3) this increase is suppressed by the simultaneous presence of a peripheral stimulus.

the rate of small saccades is suppressed by the presentation of a peripheral distractor, and the direction bias is suppressed by both the presentation of a distractor and the presentation of a parafoveal stimulus with low contrast.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms that underlie the generation of fixational eye movements.
the neural basis of visually evoked fixations and small saccades.
how the brain controls the direction and frequency of eye movements.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

fixational saccadic behavior is shaped by the interaction between two distinct neural populations, one that encodes the direction of the saccade, and the other that encodes the location of the stimulus.

the suppressive interaction is a divisive suppression that is a combination of subtractive suppression and divisive suppression of the rate and direction bias of the fixational saccadic eye movements.
fixational saccadic eye movements are influenced by suppressive interactions within a continuous visuotopic motor map.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the direction of fixational sccades are biased toward locations of the parafoveal stimuli, but the bias is modulated by the peripheral stimulus.

the direction bias of fixational sccades is shaped by the competitive interactions among neurons within a visuomotor population map, and that these interactions can be described as subtractive and divisive suppressive mechanisms.
the direction of fixational saggades is biased toward the location of a parafoveal stimulus and this bias increases with stimulus contrast.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the direction of fixational s accades is influenced by the activity of neurons that are tuned to locations of visual targets, and that the activity of these neurons is suppressed by neurons that are tuned for locations away from the visual target.

the direction of small saccades during fixation is influenced by competitive interactions within a visuomotor representation, which can be modeled by a divisive suppression of activity in the direction of the saccade.

the direction and rate of fixational eye movements are influenced by competitive interactions in the visuomotor system, similar to those that underlie large saccades, and that the strength and nature of these interactions are dependent upon the location and contrast of visual stimuli.
